Turf for Meadow Woods Pool Cages and Lanais

Turf around a Meadow Woods pool or inside a screened lanai runs within the $8–$18 per square foot market range, usually toward the upper half given the glue-down work a cage floor needs, as of September 2026. Screened pools are common on the community's 1990s and early-2000s single-story lots, where sod never held up well against the shade and edge of the enclosure anyway.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Screened pool cages are a defining feature of the older sections

Woodbridge at Meadow Woods, built in 1995 and 1996, and the surrounding single-story sections from that same stretch of construction, put up a large share of Meadow Woods' screen-enclosed pools. A cage that age is old enough that its footing and deck have settled into their final shape, which matters for turf more than it does for sod: a concrete deck inside the cage takes a glue-down install with a drainage underlay, and the crew needs a deck that isn't actively shifting for that adhesive to hold through a Central Florida summer. The narrow strip of ground outside the cage, where sod usually struggled against the shade line the screen roof casts, is where a standard turf base goes down instead.

The backing still has to drain even glued to a slab

A permeable backing built to pass more than thirty inches of water an hour matters on a Meadow Woods lanai floor for a different reason than it does on an open lawn: since the concrete slab underneath cannot absorb anything itself, the backing and the drainage underlay together are doing the entire job that native sand and rock handle everywhere else on the property. A slower or partly blocked backing on a glued floor shows up faster than the same flaw would on soil, because there is no secondary path for water to disappear into once it clears the turf.

Say you have a 480 sq ft pool deck and side strip

Say you have a 480 sq ft combination of a screened pool deck and a narrow side strip outside the cage, on a single-story home from the 1990s build-out. Within the $8–$18 market range, that project tends to land in the upper half, roughly $13 to $17 a square foot, or about $6,240 to $8,160 installed, because the glue-down work inside the cage and the drainage underlay both add labor a flat lawn doesn't need. The sprinkler zone that used to reach that strip gets capped as part of the same job, not as a separate call later.

Why the irrigation step matters more around a pool cage

A sprinkler zone that used to reach the strip beside a pool cage has to be capped once turf goes down there, since Florida's turf standard bars watering synthetic turf from an in-ground system statewide. On a Meadow Woods lot served by Orange County Utilities, that capped zone also drops out of the utility's seasonal watering-day schedule entirely, which simplifies the yard's water plan rather than complicating it: fewer zones to track, and the pool deck's turf gets by on an occasional hose rinse instead.

A clogged deck drain from infill that migrated the wrong way

Infill that washes off a Meadow Woods pool border and into the deck's own drain can back the drain up enough that water starts sheeting across the border after storms that used to clear fine, turning what started as a turf maintenance issue into standing water against the coping. Because the drain itself is shared with the pool deck's runoff generally, tracing the cause back to turf infill rather than a pool-deck plumbing problem can take longer than it should. A border sloped toward a drain is worth checking for infill buildup at the drain grate specifically, not just for thinning infill across the turf itself.

Why a lanai floor skips the rock base entirely

A screen enclosure or lanai floor around a Meadow Woods pool is almost always bare concrete, so there is no soil underneath to build a normal base from. Instead of two to four inches of washed, open-graded crushed rock, the crew glues a thin drainage underlay straight to the slab, and that underlay carries splash and rinse water sideways toward whatever drain the deck already uses. An open border between the same cage and a side fence still gets the standard rock base, graded one to two percent, because that strip sits on native sand able to take water straight down. Two areas on one Meadow Woods property, built on completely different foundations underneath the same green surface.

Keeping turf away from a pool's equipment pad and bond beam

The grading question around a pool is different from a plain lawn. Turf outside a cage has to slope away from the pool's bond beam and stay clear of the equipment pad, both to keep water from pooling against the shell and to leave the pump and filter reachable for service. On Meadow Woods' flat, poorly drained flatwoods soil, that grading takes more deliberate planning than it would on a lot with natural fall away from the structure, since there's little slope already doing that work.

Keeping crew staging off a marked septic lid during a multi-day build

Once a Meadow Woods property's septic lid location is flagged before a pool-area turf project starts, keeping material pallets, equipment, and foot traffic off that exact spot for the rest of a multi-day build matters as much as designing the border around it in the first place. A lid that was correctly avoided in the final layout can still end up buried under staged rock or turf rolls left sitting on it overnight if nobody on site remembers where it is. A visible stake or cone marking the spot through the whole job keeps the plan intact from the first day to the last.

Rechecking a septic lid's clearance years after a pool project

A septic lid marked and protected during a Meadow Woods pool-area turf build is worth rechecking periodically in the years afterward, since new landscaping, a stored pool float, or equipment added near the pump pad over time can gradually encroach on a spot nobody's paying close attention to anymore. Confirming the lid is still visible and clear takes only a minute during any other routine check of the border or lanai floor, and it's far easier than rediscovering the location from scratch the day a pump-out truck actually needs it. This matters most on properties where the original construction notes have long since been forgotten.

Questions people ask

Does a 1990s Meadow Woods pool cage need special turf preparation?

The deck itself needs checking for settling before turf glues down, but the turf system is otherwise a standard glue-down build over concrete with a drainage underlay, regardless of the cage's age.

Does capping irrigation near the pool change my Orange County Utilities bill?

It removes that zone from the watering schedule entirely, since the state rule bars in-ground irrigation on synthetic turf, but it doesn't change the rest of the property's water service.
